{{Short description|Professor of behavioural ecology}}
'''Innes C. Cuthill''' (born 1960) is a professor of [[behavioural ecology]] at the [[University of Bristol]]. His main research interest is in [[camouflage]], in particular how it evolves in response to the [[colour vision]] of other animals such as [[predator]]s.

==Life==

Cuthill was educated at [[University College School]], London. He gained a First in natural sciences (zoology) at the [[University of Cambridge]], graduating in 1982 and gained his D.Phil. at the [[University of Oxford]] in 1985. He was a junior research fellow at [[Brasenose College, Oxford]] until 1989 when he became a lecturer at the [[University of Bristol]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Innes Cuthill |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/innes-cuthill-09421514/ |publisher=LinkedIn |access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref> He became a professor there in 1998 and was head of the School of Biological Sciences from 2008 to 2012.

==Work==

Cuthill describes himself as "wear[ing] two hats, [[behavioural ecology|behavioural ecologist]] and [[sensory ecology|sensory ecologist]]",<ref name=Bristol>{{cite web |title=Professor Innes Cuthill |url=http://www.bristol.ac.uk/biology/people/innes-c-cuthill/index.html |publisher=[[University of Bristol]] |access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref> unified by seeking to explain the "design, through [[natural selection]], of animal form and function." He states that his main research interest is the [[evolution]] of [[camouflage]] of one kind of animal, such as prey, in response to the colour vision of another kind of animal, such as a [[predator]].<ref name=Bristol/>

He has published over 250 research papers, mainly on vision and [[camouflage]],<ref name=Scholar>{{cite web |title=IC Cuthill |url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?start=0&q=%22IC+Cuthill%22&hl=en&as_sdt=1,5&as_vis=1 |publisher=Google Scholar |access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref> though he has also written on the use of [[statistics in biology]], cited over 2700 times,<ref name="NakagawaCuthill2007"></ref><ref name=Scholar/> and was co-author of the ARRIVE and ARRIVE2 guidelines for reporting the use of animals in research, cited over 10,000 times.<ref name="KilkennyBrowne2010">{{cite journal |last1=Kilkenny |first1=Carol |last2=Browne |first2=William J. |last3=Cuthill |first3=Innes C. |last4=Emerson |first4=Michael |last5=Altman |first5=Douglas G. |title=Improving Bioscience Research Reporting: The ARRIVE Guidelines for Reporting Animal Research |journal=[[PLOS Biology]] |volume=8 |issue=6 |year=2010 |article-number=e1000412 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1000412|pmc=2893951 |pmid=20613859 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Scholar/>

==Awards and distinctions==

Cuthill won the Scientific Medal of the [[Zoological Society of London]] in 1998, the [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] and [[NESTA]] award for mentoring in science in 2005. From 2007 to 2010 he was president of the Association for the Study of Animal Behaviour.<ref name=Camolab>{{cite web|title=Professor Innes Cuthill|url=http://camolab.com/members/innes.php|publisher=Camolab}}</ref> He gave the [[Tinbergen Lecture]] of 2014 <ref>{{cite web|title=Tinbergen Lecturer|url=http://www.asab.org/tinbergen-lecturer/|publisher=ASAB|access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref> and won the 2018 ASAB medal for contributions to the science of animal behaviour.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tinbergen Medal|url=https://www.asab.org/asab-medal/|publisher=ASAB|access-date=12 November 2018}}</ref> He was a Fellow of the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin (Institute of Advanced Studies) from 2015-16. Nakagawa & Cuthill (2007) was selected by Biological Reviews as one of their highlight papers of the last 200 years <ref name="NakagawaCuthill2007">{{cite journal |last1=Nakagawa |first1=Shinichi |last2=Cuthill |first2=Innes C. |title=Effect size, confidence interval and statistical significance: a practical guide for biologists |journal=[[Biological Reviews]] |volume=82 |issue=4 |year=2007 |pages=591–605 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-185X.2007.00027.x |pmid=17944619|s2cid=615371 }}</ref><ref name=Scholar/>
